newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup-Rocky reforms.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup-Rocky reforms.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
John Howard has returned from his two-and-a-half week overseas trip apparently full of big ideas for more economic reform.
At least that's the impression he created, albeit temporarily. The reality is much more prosaic -- his big ideas are, in fact, big talk, with no strategy to back it up.

This is now a familiar pattern. The Prime Minister's substitute for reform is debate. It's his way of avoiding the opprobrium if the electorate decides it's sick of reform, or doesn't fancy his brand of it.
The latest example is Howard's public musing on Australia's wage structure and its relationship with the unemployment rate.
He developed this theme in Washington. People often asked him, he claimed, why Australia's unemployment rate was much higher than that of the U.S.

The explanation, he said, was the Australian ethos, which he understood, was for higher minimum wage rates than the U.S. Over and over he emphasised this was our ethos, but, in effect, it came at the cost of higher unemployment.

When he returned to Australia, he continued making this point. Quite naturally, eventually two newspapers drew the reasonable conclusion that he meant to do something about it, given his concern about our continuing high jobless level.

They couldn't have been more off the beam. After a week of pushing this line, Howard was finally asked to clarify. Question: "Prime Minister, should Australians be prepared to take lower wages in the interest of creating more jobs?" Answer: "Look, I'm not arguing that we should cut minimum wages, let me make that clear. What I'm saying is that one of the reasons that unemployment in the United States is lower than it is in Australia is because traditionally America's minimum wage structure has been different, but I'm not saying that the Australian ethos, which is that if you get a job you should have a decent minimum wage, I don't think that ethos should be altered."
So, essentially, there was a lot of fuss about nothing. The prime minister has no intention of trying to do anything about the minimum wage because he realises it's a political no-no.
But it does have one purpose. It provides an excuse why the Howard government might fail to meet community expectations in improving the unemployment picture.
This week saw the release of another monthly set of labour force figures which offered no sign of recovery.

Sure the jobless rate was down, from 8.8 to 8.5 percent for June, but so was the participation rate, to 63.0 percent, the lowest since the end of 1994 and comparing poorly to the 63.75 percent forecast in the budget.
At the forecast participation level, the unemployment rate would be over nine percent.
So the heat is being gradually turned up on the government.

Howard himself is now saying there should be a fall in the jobless rate "next year". That will be two years into his administration's first term and at about the point where the electorate will be asking even more seriously why the much vaunted boosts for small business have failed to bear fruit in job creation.
When Howard is comparing the U.S. and Australian unemployment rates, one stark economic difference he has not mentioned is growth.
America's annualised GDP growth in its latest term came in at 5.9 percent, against Australia's rather desultory 2.4 percent.
But any reform ideas which may get that growth moving will be approached with extreme caution by this government. Tax reform is its biggest test.

Howard's rhetoric on tax was cranked up during his overseas trip. In the past five months a tax shake-up has progressed, in Howard's own words, from something which was a long way short of economic elixir to the last great unfinished reform.
But how will Howard handle it from here? He told journalists in New York that he would soon be calling his cabinet together for a brainstorming session on the next move in the reform process.
This is likely to expose the cracks in the ministry over the goods and services tax (GST).

Howard wants one, but isn't game enough to say so publicly. Treasurer Peter Costello wants the GST you have when you're not having a GST -- a separate services tax combined with a clean-up of the wholesale sales tax.
Howard wants to use the GST to cut income tax rates; Costello doesn't want to spend any of the prospective surplus to sweeten the tax reform pill.

With Howard's confusing approach to reform, involving regular kite flying followed by sudden retreats, combined with fundamental disagreement over the preferred strategy, are ingredients for another rocky ride on the tax reform cart.
-- Reuter Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
